title: Building Your Data Science Portfolio
summary: Skills only get you hired if others can see them, and a portfolio is how a beginner data scientist proves capability without prior job experience. A strong portfolio isn't a pile of tutorials redone; it's a small set of two to four polished projects
content:
# Building Your Data Science Portfolio ##### Twelve projects, zero callbacks A career-changer in Kochi applied to 60 data science roles over four months. Her GitHub had twelve repositories: Titanic survival, MNIST digits, Iris classification, Boston housing, a movie recommender, a stock price predictor, and six more. Zero callbacks. A mentor looked at her GitHub and identified the problem in about ninety seconds. Every project was a tutorial reproduction on a benchmark dataset. Every repository had a default README. There was no live demo, no business framing, and — critically — nothing that distinguished her from the thousands of other candidates who had also done Titanic. She deleted nine repositories, rebuilt two, and added one new project using messy data she scraped herself with a deployed app. Three projects. Eleven applications. Four callbacks. The portfolio is not a record of everything you have learned. It is **evidence, curated for a specific reader with thirty seconds of attention.** ##### What actually gets evaluated Understanding the reviewer's constraints changes what you build. A hiring manager screening sixty applications spends roughly twenty seconds per GitHub profile and two minutes on one repository if something catches their attention. They are scanning for signals that you can do the job, not reading your code. | Signal | What it demonstrates | How obvious it is | |---|---|---| | **A live demo that loads** | You can ship, not just analyse | Instant | | **Messy real data** | You have handled reality | Visible in the README | | **A business framing** | You understand why work matters | First paragraph | | **Honest limitations** | Judgement and self-awareness | Rare, memorable | | **Clean commit history** | You work like an engineer | One click | | **Reproducible setup** | Someone else could use this | Tested in 60 seconds | | Tutorial dataset | Nothing — thousands have done it | Instant negative | | Notebook-only, no README | You have not shipped anything | Instant negative | The asymmetry matters: negative signals are detected faster than positive ones. A repository with no README is dismissed in five seconds; a good project needs the README to earn the two minutes. ##### Choosing projects Four criteria. A project needs at least three. **1. Real, messy data you obtained yourself.** Scraped, API-collected, or a genuinely messy public dataset. Kaggle competition data is acceptable; Iris and Titanic are not, because the cleaning work — the part that demonstrates competence — has already been done for you. **2. A plausible decision behind it.** "Predicting X" is a task. "Helping a retention team prioritise 200 monthly calls" is a project. The second frames every subsequent choice. **3. One genuinely hard component.** Class imbalance, a latency constraint, multilingual text, a messy multi-table join, temporal validation, deployment under memory limits. Something that generated a real problem you solved. **4. Explainable in ninety seconds** to someone non-technical. Project ideas using data you can actually get in India: | Project | Data source | Hard part | |---|---|---| | Consumer complaint routing | Public grievance portals | Hinglish text, class imbalance | | Mandi price forecasting | Agmarknet (data.gov.in) | Time series, unit errors, seasonality | | Air quality prediction | CPCB open data | Station gaps, temporal features | | Job posting skill extraction | Scraped listings (check ToS) | NER, deduplication at scale | | Electricity demand forecast | State load despatch data | Strong seasonality, weather joins | | Cricket win probability | Cricsheet ball-by-ball | Sequential features, leakage traps | | Local transit delay prediction | GTFS feeds | Real-time data, geospatial | The strongest differentiator is **data nobody else has**. A project on scraped local data — Pune restaurant prices, Maharashtra school enrolment, a specific industry's job postings — is automatically unique, and the collection work is itself a demonstrated skill. **Two to four projects, well-built, beats twelve.** Reviewers do not average your work; they judge you by the best one they actually look at, and twelve repositories means they pick one at random and it is probably not your best. A useful portfolio shape: ``` 1. Capstone — end-to-end, deployed, business-framed [the centrepiece] 2. Different domain — NLP, time series, or computer vision 3. Different skill — a dashboard, a data pipeline, or an OSS contribution ``` ##### The README as a case study This is where most of the value is created, and it takes an hour. ```markdown # Mandi Price Forecasting for Onion Traders **[▶ Live app](https://mandi-forecast.streamlit.app)** · [Report](reports/report.md) · [3-min video](https://...) Forecasts onion modal prices 7 days ahead across 12 Maharashtra mandis, helping farmers decide whether to sell now or wait. **Result:** MASE 0.79 against a seasonal-naive baseline — 21% lower error than the standard benchmark. On a 100-quintal lot, better timing is worth approximately ₹8,000–14,000. ![Forecast screenshot](reports/figures/forecast.png) ## Why this problem Farmers sell into price volatility with no forward visibility. Selling a week early or late can change realised price by 15–30%. Agmarknet publishes daily prices, but raw daily numbers do not tell you what happens next week. ## Data Agmarknet, 2021–2026, 183,402 rows across 12 mandis. | Issue found | Scale | Resolution | |---|---|---| | Price recorded per kg not per quintal | 11.2% of rows | Detected via bimodal histogram; ×100 | | Mandi name variants | 340 strings → 12 mandis | Built and reviewed a mapping table | | Missing days cluster at festivals | 4.7% of days | Treated as closures, not imputed | | min/max price leak the target | r > 0.98 | Excluded from features | ## Approach Seasonal-naive baseline → lag and rolling features → LightGBM with temporal cross-validation → quantile models for prediction intervals. | Model | MASE | 80% interval coverage | |---|---|---| | Seasonal naive | 1.00 | — | | Linear + lags | 0.94 | 71% | | **LightGBM** | **0.79** | **78%** | ## What I got wrong My first version used `TimeSeriesSplit` but built rolling features across the full series before splitting — leaking future information. MASE looked like 0.61. Recomputing features inside each fold gave the honest 0.79. The bug took two days to find and is the reason I now build every transformation inside a pipeline. ## Limitations - Accuracy degrades beyond a 7-day horizon (MASE 0.94 at 14 days). - Onion only; other crops have different seasonality. - No weather data — adding rainfall would likely improve the monsoon period. - Cannot anticipate policy shocks (export bans moved prices 40% in 2023). ## Reproduce ```bash git clone ... && cd mandi-forecast python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python -m src.train # ~2 min on the sample data streamlit run app.py ``` ``` What makes that work: the **demo link is above the fold**, the **result is quantified in business terms**, the **data issues table** demonstrates real cleaning work in one glance, and the **"What I got wrong"** section shows judgement no metric can. That last section deserves emphasis. Almost nobody includes it. It signals that you debug your own work rather than trusting the first good number, and interviewers consistently ask about it — which means you get to discuss a topic you have prepared thoroughly. ##### GitHub profile Your profile is the first page a reviewer sees. ```markdown ### Hi, I'm Ananya 👋 Data scientist based in Pune, focused on forecasting and applied ML for Indian agriculture and retail. Previously a supply-chain analyst — I move between the data and the operations side. **Currently:** building time-series forecasting tools · learning causal inference ### Featured projects **[Mandi Price Forecasting](link)** · [live demo](link) 7-day onion price forecasts across 12 Maharashtra mandis. MASE 0.79 vs seasonal naive. *Python, LightGBM, Streamlit* **[Complaint Routing Classifier](link)** · [live demo](link) Routes Hinglish consumer complaints to the right department with 0.87 macro-F1 across 9 classes. *scikit-learn, TF-IDF, FastAPI* **[Air Quality Dashboard](link)** · [live demo](link) Interactive CPCB data explorer covering 40 Indian cities. *Plotly, Streamlit* ### Skills Python · SQL · Pandas · scikit-learn · LightGBM · Streamlit · Git 📫 [LinkedIn](link) · [Email](mailto:) · [Blog](link) ``` Practical steps that take ten minutes each: **pin your best repositories** (up to six, and use three or four), **write a description and add topics** to every pinned repo, **use a real photo**, and — genuinely underrated — **make sure your commit history is not all on one day**, because a project committed in a single burst reads as a tutorial follow-along. ##### Blogging and Kaggle Optional, and valuable when done specifically. **Writing** works when it teaches something non-obvious you learned by debugging. "Introduction to Random Forests" competes with ten thousand identical posts. "The leakage bug that made my time-series model look 23% better than it was" is unique, useful, and directly demonstrates competence. Two or three genuinely good posts beat twenty generic ones. Publish on your own site, dev.to, or Medium — the platform matters far less than whether the content is worth reading. **Kaggle** signals a narrower skill than a shipped project. A competition medal proves modelling ability and proves nothing about problem framing, data collection, stakeholder communication or deployment. It is a reasonable supplement and a poor substitute. The Kaggle activity that transfers best is writing well-explained public notebooks — that is teaching, which is the same skill as documentation. **Open-source contributions** are undervalued relative to their signal. A merged pull request to pandas, scikit-learn, Evidently or Streamlit proves you can read someone else's code, follow a review process, and write something to a maintained standard. The path in: use the project, find a real friction point, open a well-written issue, fix a `good-first-issue`, then fix something you personally needed. ##### Where the portfolio goes ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Portfolio: 2-4 strong projects] --> B[GitHub profile README
pinned repos] A --> C[LinkedIn: featured section,
project links in About] A --> D[CV: one line per project
with the result] A --> E[Optional: personal site] B --> F[Applications] C --> F D --> F E --> F F --> G[Interview: you drive the
conversation to your work] ``` On a CV, each project gets one line stating the **outcome**, not the tools: ``` Mandi Price Forecasting — 7-day onion price forecasts across 12 Maharashtra mandis; MASE 0.79 vs seasonal-naive baseline; deployed Streamlit app ``` Not: "Used Python, Pandas, scikit-learn and LightGBM to build a model." The tools are visible in the repository. The CV line has one job: make the reader click. ##### The one-hour upgrade If you have existing projects and limited time, this ordering gives the most improvement per hour: 1. **Delete tutorial projects.** Titanic, Iris, MNIST. Removing them raises your average. 2. **Write one proper README** for your best project — problem, result with a number, screenshot, reproduce steps. 3. **Deploy that project.** Streamlit Cloud takes twenty minutes and adds the strongest single signal. 4. **Add a "What I got wrong" section.** Ten minutes, disproportionate impact. 5. **Pin the good repos** and write the profile README. 6. **Test your own reproduce instructions** in a fresh clone. That sequence is roughly four hours and it is the difference between the Kochi candidate's first four months and her fifth. ##### Common mistakes - Twelve tutorial projects instead of three real ones. - Benchmark datasets where the hard work is already done. - No README, or a README containing only the project name. - No deployed demo. - Leading with tools rather than the problem and the result. - No limitations section, so nothing signals judgement. - Reproduce instructions that were never tested. - Notebooks committed with outputs and no narrative. - All commits on a single day. - A profile with no pinned repositories and no description. ##### Hands-on Audit your existing projects honestly against the four criteria and delete anything that meets fewer than three. Then take your best remaining project and rewrite its README as a case study: demo link and result in the first three lines, a data-issues table, an approach section with a results comparison, a "What I got wrong" section, honest limitations, and tested reproduce instructions. Pin it on GitHub and write your profile README. For the mini-project, build a simple personal portfolio — a GitHub profile README is sufficient, or a lightweight static site if you prefer. Showcase two to four projects with descriptions, screenshots and links to live demos. Then get external feedback: show it to someone who hires, or post it for review, and specifically ask them what they understood about your capabilities after thirty seconds. The gap between what you emphasised and what they perceived is the actionable feedback. For the assignment, write a one-paragraph case study for your capstone suitable for the top of its README, framing the problem, approach and result for a recruiter. Constrain yourself to four sentences and include one number. Then read it aloud — if it sounds like a description of what you did rather than what you achieved, rewrite it. ##### Key takeaways - Reviewers spend seconds, not minutes — curate two to four strong projects rather than accumulating twelve. - Real messy data, a business framing, and a working demo link are the three strongest signals. - The README is the product: result first, screenshot visible, reproduce steps tested. - A "What I got wrong" section demonstrates judgement more effectively than any metric, and almost nobody writes one. - Lead with outcomes rather than tools everywhere — CV, LinkedIn, profile and README.
